cim: How to AI Face Swap a Photo, Step by Step
cim_eredeti: How to AI Face Swap a Photo, Step by Step
szoveg_eredeti:
An AI face swap replaces the face in one photo with a face from a second photo, and matches the target photo’s pose, expression, lighting, and skin tone. On Krea that is two uploads and one button, at AI Face Swap. The tool works on still photos. The same page lists dedicated video and GIF face swaps as coming soon.

You only need a photo that already has a face (the target) and a clear photo of the face you want to use (the source). No layers, masks, or desktop editor.

Left: the target photo from Krea’s face swap page. Right: the generated face swap. The shirt, pose, and background stay; the face, hair, and glasses change. Both images are the pair published on the app.

A face swap photo is not a new portrait from scratch. The scene stays the scene. Krea’s face swap page describes the edit this way: the source face is blended into the target photo while the target’s pose, expression, lighting, and skin tone are matched. The page also says the tool maps facial geometry so the new face fits the target’s angle.

What the published example actually changes is worth seeing before you rely on it. In the portrait above, the white shirt and blue background stay. The hair goes from straight to curly, and the glasses disappear. Treat hair, glasses, and other accessories as things to check, not as a guarantee either way.

The page says the strongest results are single-subject portraits. Group photos can come back inconsistent when faces are small or overlapping.

The target is the photo you want to keep: the pose, the clothes, the room, the framing. On the app it is labeled Target Image, with the hint “Upload the photo with face to replace.”

Pick a frame where the face is large enough to see and not blocked by a hand, a phone, or heavy shadow. A sharp photo beats a screenshot. If the only file you have is blurry, noisy, or tiny, fix that first. How to improve photo quality covers unblur and upscale, and how to restore old photos covers scratches and tears on a print. A face swap cannot recover detail the file never had.

The source is the face you want to insert. On the app it is labeled Your Photo, with the hint “Upload the face you want to insert.”

Use a photo where the face is clear, high resolution, evenly lit, and not covered by sunglasses, a mask, or hair across the eyes. The app’s own tip is to choose a target whose angle is similar to the source. A front-facing source dropped onto a sharp profile has less real information to match, and the blend has to invent more.

Only upload a face you have the right to use. That means your own face, or someone who agreed. The consent rules are in the section below.

Click Face Swap. The control on the page is marked 2 CU (compute units). The page says most generations finish within a few seconds, depending on image size and complexity, and that you do not mask or composite by hand.

The same page says the tool is free to use, that uploads are not used to train Krea’s models, and that the output is high resolution. It does not publish a pixel size for that output, so “high resolution” here means the claim on the app, not a specific width.

If the first result looks slightly off, run it again with the same two photos, or swap in a clearer source. A second pass is normal. Face edits are sensitive to the source crop.

The before-and-after pair shipped with the face swap app. The blazer, shirt, and background stay. The face is replaced.

The face swap page offers two next steps after the image is done: continue in the AI image editor or enhance the result. In the blog’s usual paths those are Krea Edit and the Enhancer.

Use Edit when one thing is wrong and the rest is right: a stray edge along the jaw, a background you want changed, a lighting pass. How to edit and stylize a photo with AI walks through that kind of follow-up edit. Use the Enhancer when the swap looks right but you need a larger file for a print or a layout.

The face swap page also links image to image for a restyle after the swap. That is a separate edit, not part of the face swap click.

Upload a target photo and a source face. Krea's AI face swap runs in the browser, and the page says you can start without an account.

The app’s FAQ gives the practical bar: a clear, high-resolution source face, good lighting, little obstruction, and a target where the face is visible at a similar angle. Clearer inputs produce a more natural blend.

A few capture habits matter more than any slider:

The face swap page groups the job into four uses. All of them are still photos.

These four frames are the style examples published on the face swap page. They show the same kind of output the app is selling: a face carried into a different grade, from golden-hour blossoms to a cool haze.

Labeled on the app, left to right, top to bottom: Cinematic Bloom, Retro Prism, Street Portrait, Dream Haze.

A realistic face swap is easy to mistake for a real photo. That is the point of the tool, and it is also the limit.

Krea’s terms prohibit content that is fraudulent, deceptive, or otherwise objectionable, and they name a specific case: “actions and content which impersonate individuals without their consent (e.g. deepfakes).” The same terms say you will not use content you do not own without the owner’s prior consent, or in a way that violates someone else’s rights. Sexually graphic content is prohibited. A violation is grounds for losing access.

This guide does not cover video face swap, because the app does not offer it yet. The page says photo face swap is available now, and that dedicated video and GIF workflows are coming soon.

Keep the two originals next to the result. If you later need to prove which file was the edit, the sources are the record.

Two uploads, then Face Swap. Photo only for now. Video and GIF tools are marked coming soon on the app.
